title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
The failure described here is not the crash itself but a claim about evidence. Tesla told a grieving family that the fatal crash data from its self-driving car was gone. Reporting states that a hacker then showed the data was retained in the cars, and that the recovered data showed the system detected a hazard before the fatal crash, despite the claim that it was missing. That is a false statement of absence about a record that existed.

The failure sits in the evidence-handling stage of a deployed system, after the vehicle had been sold and driven, not in the driving software at the moment of impact. The data at issue was generated by the car and stored onboard, so whether it existed was answerable by inspecting the vehicle rather than by accepting the manufacturer's account. Catching the discrepancy took an outside party with the technical means to read that storage. A jury ordered Tesla to pay more than $240 million, and a judge later upheld a $243 million verdict, with the two figures differing across reports. Court orders in the case address summary judgment, expert admissibility, and a renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law or a new trial.

What is not established is intent. A verdict upheld on review is a legal finding on liability, not proof that the data was withheld deliberately. The summary text supplied with this record is unreadable, so the specific facts of the crash and the court's reasoning are not available here.
